name: Small Talk That Works
lede: The two minutes before a meeting starts can feel like a test. Learn the small, warm phrases that fill them — and make people glad you’re there.
outcome: Warm, short, and never awkward — the phrases that make the two minutes before a meeting feel easy.
outcomes: Open a conversation with a colleague without waiting for the perfect moment.
Keep a chat going for a minute or two, then step away without it feeling odd.
Use the same phrases every week until they sound like something you’d really say.

aside.title: No scripts. Just things people actually say.
aside.body: Start with one line you feel comfortable with. The rest usually takes care of itself.

words.definition: To talk with someone about what has happened since you last spoke.
words.example: Let’s catch up for five minutes before the meeting starts.

words.definition: A friendly way to ask someone how they are doing.
words.example: Hey, how’s things with the new project so far?

words.definition: A casual question about what has changed in someone’s life.
words.example: Morning! So what’s new with you this week?

words.definition: Very busy, with too many things to do at once.
words.example: I’m slammed this morning — can we talk at lunch?

words.definition: Saturday and Sunday, when most people do not work.
words.example: Any plans for the weekend, or a quiet one?

words.definition: A day when you do not go to work.
words.example: I’m taking a day off on Friday to see family.

words.definition: Time away from work, often spent travelling or resting.
words.example: Are you going anywhere nice for your holiday?

words.definition: The journey you make to and from work each day.
words.example: How long is your commute in the morning?

words.definition: The cars and other vehicles moving along a road.
words.example: The traffic was terrible, so I’m a bit late.

words.definition: The conditions outside, such as sun, rain, or wind.
words.example: Lovely weather this morning — did you walk in?

words.definition: The meal you eat in the middle of the working day.
words.example: Do you want to grab some lunch after this?

words.definition: A hot drink many people have in the morning or at breaks.
words.example: I’m getting a coffee — can I get you one?

words.definition: A short pause from work to rest or get a drink.
words.example: Shall we take a quick break before the next call?

words.definition: Having a lot to do and not much free time.
words.example: You seem busy today — is the launch soon?

words.definition: To finish something, such as a meeting or a task.
words.example: We should wrap up soon so everyone can go.

words.definition: To start something, especially a meeting or an event.
words.example: Shall we kick off once the whole team is here?

words.definition: To come into a meeting, group, or conversation.
words.example: Do you want to join us for coffee?

words.definition: To tell people someone’s name when they meet for the first time.
words.example: Let me introduce you to Priya from design.

words.definition: To see and talk to someone for the first time.
words.example: Good to meet you — I’ve heard a lot about you.

words.definition: A polite thing to say when you meet someone for the first time.
words.example: Nice to meet you — I’m on the product team.

words.definition: A short way to ask the other person the same question.
words.example: I’m ready for the weekend — how about you?

words.definition: A friendly way to agree to a plan or suggestion.
words.example: Coffee at eleven? Sounds good — see you there.

words.definition: To ask someone to tell you something later.
words.example: Let me know if you’re free for lunch.

words.definition: A casual way to say goodbye, with no fixed next meeting.
words.example: I’m off to a call — see you around.
